title: Vand chhako, deeper
hookLine: sharing as the shape of a life, not a donation

cards: A boy is handed a bag of coins and sent to market. His father's instruction is simple: make a good deal, a true bargain, something that will turn a profit.
On the road, the story says, the boy meets holy men who have gone without food. He looks at the coins, and at them, buys food and feeds them, and walks home with an empty bag. His father is furious.
The boy is Nanak, and the story gives his answer: that was the true bargain, sacha sauda, the true deal. Today, the third of the three phrases.

teach.b: Vand chhako. Vand means divide, share out. Chhako means eat, take your portion.
The order is the teaching: share, and eat. Not eat, and then give away whatever's left over. The sharing is built into the meal itself.
That's the difference between a donation and a shape. A donation is something you do once in a while, on top of a life. A shape is the life.
Guru Nanak's salok from two days ago already holds it: the one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives something from his hand, recognizes the path. Earning and giving, in one breath.
And Sikh life made that shape visible.

Tradition says Guru Nanak's community at Kartarpur farmed together and ate together, and it traces langar, the free kitchen, to that: a meal served to anyone who walks in, everyone on the same floor, eating the same food.
Nobody fills out a form to prove they're hungry. Nobody is asked their faith. That's vand chhako at the scale of a community.
The Sacha Sauda story makes the same point in one afternoon. The father wanted a deal that turned a profit. The boy saw a deal that fed people, and called that the true one.
So the deeper version of sharing isn't how much you give.
It's whether giving comes first, before the asking, before the leftovers, before anyone has to explain themselves.

how: Sikhs practice vand chhako through langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara where anyone may eat, through seva, and through dasvandh, setting aside a portion of what they earn to share.

o: eat first, then give away what is left
fast one day a week to feed the poor
share out what you have, and eat together

games.q: vand chhako, opened up: tap the pairs.

s: vand chhako means give away whatever is left after you eat
the order is the teaching: share, and eat; the sharing is part of the meal.
in the story, young Nanak spends his father's money feeding hungry holy men
he called it the true bargain, Sacha Sauda.
at langar, people are asked their faith before they eat
anyone who walks in is served, all on the same floor.

games.q: your father sends you to market with coins to make a profitable deal. on the road you meet holy men who haven't eaten. what do you do?
o: make the deal, then give them what's left.
buy them food with all of it.
promise to come back with food tomorrow.
games.why: the story says young Nanak fed them with the money and came home empty-handed, calling it the true bargain.

practice: Let one person come to mind who could use something you have, not necessarily money: time, a meal, a ride, a skill, a phone call, attention.
Notice whether they would ever ask, since some people never do, and picture yourself offering it before they have to. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.

wordCard.voice: Vand chhako. Share, and eat: the sharing built into the meal and into the shape of a life, not added afterward. Today's word.

orig.note: vand is to share out; chhako is to eat, take your portion.

carryVoice: Your line: share first. The true bargain is the one that feeds someone. See you tomorrow.
